SCENE CONTEXT
Night, the backyard pool party — the same night as the opening hook, now with its ending. Jenny gets a red punch, trades compliments with two friends and watches Chen, Enjee and Ryan laughing by the back door until Mark in his horse mask knocks her into the pool. Chen helps her out; Ryan and Enjee share a shy look, and the camera pulls back to a wide view of the house.

ACTIVE REFERENCES
<<<image_1>>> — JENNY. Face, long wavy ash-brown hair with blunt bangs and costume 100% match the reference: white bunny costume — fluffy bunny-ear headband, sparkly white dress with fluffy trim, white knee-high boots. Clean makeup — rosy blush, soft pink lips, no fake blood anywhere.
<<<image_2>>> — ENJEE. Face, long straight black hair and costume 100% match the reference: pink cupcake hat with a big bow, white-and-pink striped puff-sleeve romper with pink heart buttons.
<<<image_3>>> — RYAN. Face, messy black hair and costume 100% match the reference: thin black metal glasses with clear lenses, natural-looking red contact lenses, drawn stitch scars on his forehead, cheek and around his neck, navy blazer, white shirt, long red satin necktie, charcoal shorts with a silver chain.
<<<image_4>>> — CHEN. Face, hair (black with bleached-blonde ends) and costume 100% match the reference: oxblood velvet vampire cape, black leather coat, open black shirt, small fangs.
<<<image_5>>> — MARK. Brown rubber horse-head mask, beige plaid short-sleeve shirt with a plaid tie, green chinos, red sneakers. The mask stays on.
<<<image_6>>> — PARTY GUESTS. Costume style for all extras; every guest looks different and wears a different costume; none of them is a main character. Among them: a waiter in white mummy bandages with a tray of red punch cups, and Jenny's two girlfriends — a witch in a black lace dress and a girl with cat ears.
<<<image_7>>> — LOCATION: BACKYARD. A long glowing-blue pool leading to the purple-lit back of the house: a porch with a few steps and an open back door glowing with warm light, a giant dark octopus over the roof, jack-o'-lanterns lining both decks, white ghosts hanging in the trees.
Reference sheets show one person from several angles; ignore studio backdrops.

LOCATION MAP
The pool runs straight out from the back porch into the garden. Jenny comes out of the back door, walks down the porch steps and along one deck to a spot halfway down the pool, right at the edge — the water directly at her right side — and turns to face the house. Later Chen, Enjee and Ryan stand together on the porch by the back door, about 12 m from her. Guests crowd both decks, chatting and drinking. Mark comes running along Jenny's deck from the garden end, behind her.

FIRST FRAME
Medium-wide from the pool deck at chest height, looking at the back of the house: the back door swings open and Jenny steps out onto the porch into the party — guests chatting and laughing all around the glowing pool, pumpkins along the decks.

FORMAT MODE
Multi-shot sequence, 30 seconds, hard cuts; the last shot is one continuous move.

ACTION TIMING
SHOT 1 (0–3 s) — 63°. Jenny steps out of the back door and down the porch steps into the party. The mummy waiter passes with his tray of red punch, serving guests, and holds the tray out to her; she takes a cup with a small nod.
SHOT 2 (3–7 s) — 47°, two-shot on the deck. Her two girlfriends catch her as she walks; the witch girl, delighted: "Oh my God, Jenny — your costume is so cute tonight!" Jenny smiles: "Aw, thanks — yours too!" The two wave and drift off into the crowd.
SHOT 3 (7–9 s) — 29°, telephoto, Jenny's point of view across the pool: on the porch by the open back door, Chen, Enjee and Ryan stand together, talking and laughing — Chen gesturing big, Enjee laughing, Ryan smiling at her. Sharp focus, natural colors.
SHOT 4 (9–11.5 s) — 47°, medium close-up of Jenny at the pool edge, camera in front of her, the pool on screen-left. She sips the punch, eyes fixed on the porch; she takes another sip, fingers tightening on the cup.
SHOT 5 (11.5–13 s) — 47°, close-up, handheld tracking alongside Mark: he breaks into a run along the deck toward her, whooping, arms pumping, the rubber mask bouncing.
SHOT 6 (13–15.5 s) — 47°, profile from the opposite deck, like the opening hook: Jenny at the edge facing screen-right, cup at her lips; Mark runs in from screen-left behind her and slams into her left shoulder. She tips toward the camera; one second of smooth slow motion as she falls with the cup, the red punch spilling out in an arc — then a full-speed heavy splash.
SHOT 7 (15.5–17 s) — 63°, on the porch: Chen, Enjee and Ryan freeze mid-laugh in shock — Enjee's hands fly to her mouth, Ryan's eyes go wide, Chen's jaw drops.
SHOT 8 (17–18.5 s) — 63°: Chen jumps down the porch steps and runs along the deck toward the pool, cape flying.
SHOT 9 (18.5–21 s) — 47°, at water level: Jenny bursts up through the surface inside a soft round patch of red punch, gasping, wet hair plastered to her face, bunny ears drooping. Furious, she swims to the edge with hard, angry strokes.
SHOT 10 (21–24.5 s) — 47°, close-up at the pool edge: Jenny grabs the edge, catching her breath; a hand reaches into frame right in front of her. Her eyes follow it up and the camera tilts up with her eyeline — Chen is crouched at the edge, offering his hand. Her glare softens into a small smile, and she puts her hand in his.
SHOT 11 (24.5–30 s) — 63°, one continuous move. It starts on a medium two-shot of Ryan and Enjee on the porch, watching. Their eyes drift from the pool to each other; when their eyes meet, they both look away with shy smiles, then sneak another look. At 27 s the camera pulls back smoothly and rises into a high wide view of the house: the purple-lit back of the house with the octopus on the roof, the glowing pool and the crowd all around it. Jenny and Chen are hidden in the crowd, out of view.

ACTING TASK (each character is fully invested in a tactic; the work happens in the eyes):
SCENE DIRECTION (shared, unspoken): keep the party fun — whatever happens, roll with it.
JENNY — MOTIVE: pride; she refuses to be the girl who lost. GOAL: hold it together while watching the three of them. OBSTACLE: their easy laughter on the porch. TACTIC: she plays the confident queen with her friends; alone at the edge she sips the punch to give her face something to do, eyes stealing to Chen and Enjee. In the water she attacks the pool to get out on her own; when she sees the hand is Chen's, she checks his eyes for mockery, finds none, and lets a small smile through.
CHEN — MOTIVE: he's the host, and he cares. GOAL: get her out and make sure she's okay. TACTIC: he crouches low to meet her eyes and offers his hand without a trace of a laugh.
ENJEE and RYAN — MOTIVE: each wants to know if the other feels it too. GOAL: share the moment without getting caught looking first. TACTIC: they pretend to watch the pool, steal glances, hold eye contact for one beat, then look away smiling.
MARK — pure party joy; he runs without looking.
GIRLFRIENDS and GUESTS — party talk; the girls hype Jenny up, the guests gasp at the splash.
(Safety: gaze always engaged in the task — never a frozen, glassy, unfocused stare; natural blink cadence, actors blink now and then to moisturize their eyes.)

PHYSICS
Real weight in the bump: Mark's momentum knocks her off balance at the wet edge. The punch arc breaks into droplets; heavy splash, spray, spreading rings. The punch spreads in the water as a soft round cloud. Surfacing: water sheets off her head, wet hair clings, the soaked fluffy trim hangs heavy, her strokes throw up spray. Chen's grip is firm; the velvet cape swings and settles as he runs and crouches.

LIGHTING
Night exterior lit by practicals: purple uplights on the house, warm white light from the open back door and the porch, orange jack-o'-lantern glow along the decks, underwater pool lights throwing blue caustics. Chen, Enjee and Ryan on the porch are lit by the warm white porch light, sharp and true-colored — no pink glow, pink tint or dreamy haze on them. Faces readable; deep natural shadows.

AUDIO
Party music from outdoor speakers, chatter and laughter around the pool, distant laughter from the porch. Mark's whoop, the thud of the impact, a heavy splash, gasps. Jenny's sharp gasp as she surfaces and the slap of her angry strokes. The music plays on and swells gently as the camera pulls back. Dialogue in natural, casual native American English with no accent, exact lines only: the witch girl — bubbly, excited young female voice; Jenny — confident, polished young female voice. No narration, no subtitles.

STYLE
Glossy teen K-drama payoff: Halloween purple, pumpkin orange and pool blue, a comic splash, then a warm, sweet ending; clean digital cinema image, fine grain, high contrast with readable faces.

QUALITY
Natural 180-degree shutter motion cadence: running and the fall carry realistic motion blur, faces sharp at hold points; the slow-motion beat and the final pull-back are smooth; stable picture, no ghosting, no flicker, no duplicated limbs.

POSITIVE CONSTRAINTS
Exactly five named characters: Jenny, Enjee, Ryan, Chen and Mark; the mummy waiter and the two girlfriends are extras. Jenny's face and costume stay clean — no blood. Chen, Enjee and Ryan always appear in natural colors without any pink glow. The pool is at Jenny's right side and she falls into the water. The final wide shows the house and the crowd around the pool, with Jenny and Chen out of view. Jenny is the only bunny, Mark the only horse mask, Chen the only vampire, Enjee the only cupcake costume.

SCENE CONTEXT
Daytime at school. Enjee is walking down the corridor when a plastic Halloween skeleton drops out of the ceiling right into her face — somebody's prank — and she jumps out of her skin. She bats it away and walks on. A second later a group text from Chen lands: the notification sounds arrive one after another, each student reaching for their phone only after their own sound has gone off. Enjee is the last. She stops and reads hers, calmly, giving nothing away. Hard cut straight into a four-way split screen of four friends, the quarters popping in one at a time with no pauses, each person speaking and then carrying straight on with whatever they were doing. Fifteen seconds, nine timed shots.

ACTIVE REFERENCES
<<<image_1>>> — MARK in school clothes, 100% matches: messy dark hair, small earrings, worn grey-brown jacket over a black button vest, white shirt, striped tie, studded belt, ripped bootcut jeans.
<<<image_2>>> — OLIVIA in school clothes, 100% matches: very long straight black hair with sparkly jeweled clips and white ribbon bows, fluffy pink cardigan, white pleated mini skirt, silver quilted bag.
<<<image_3>>> — LOCATION, the school hallway, and the whole hallway section happens here: pastel-blue wall with turquoise lockers and gold baroque mirrors on the left, white fluted columns and pink arches on the right, a chain of crystal chandeliers down the center of the ceiling, a tall arched window with a blue balustrade at the far end, pale marble floor.
<<<image_4>>> — JENNY in school clothes, 100% matches: long ash-brown wavy hair with bangs, turquoise headband, mint leather jacket, pink crop top, purple plaid shorts, lilac shoulder bag, turquoise knee socks.
<<<image_5>>> — RYAN in school clothes, 100% matches: messy black hair, thin metal rectangular glasses, grey crewneck sweater over a white tee, light-wash flared jeans.
<<<image_6>>> — ENJEE in school clothes, 100% matches: long straight black hair with a center part, pink short-sleeve tie-front blouse over a grey polka-dot top, tiered white-and-pink lace ruffle skirt, sheer white lace stockings, pearl necklace with a pink butterfly pendant.
<<<image_7>>> — THE PHONE, and every phone in this film is this exact handset: A SHORT CHUBBY PILLOWED TILE with hugely rounded, almost quarter-circle corners, a solid opaque soft-touch pastel shell with softly domed edges and NO FLAT METAL RAIL, one single round lens in a shallow dimple in the upper left ringed by a thin glowing white halo, a small empty strap hole at the bottom left corner, and the small lowercase word "miruu" embossed tone on tone low on the back. ITS FRONT HAS A SOFT EQUAL BEZEL ALL ROUND IN THE SAME PASTEL COLOUR, generously rounded screen corners, AND NO NOTCH, NO PILL, NO ISLAND, NO PUNCH HOLE AND NO CAMERA CUT-OUT ANYWHERE IN THE DISPLAY.
Ignore grey backdrops and turnaround layouts in every reference.

THE PRANK SKELETON IN SHOT 2
A CHEAP LIFE-SIZE PLASTIC HALLOWEEN SKELETON, bone-white, a few feet of it visible — skull, ribcage and dangling arms — hanging head-down from A THIN BLACK CORD tied around its ribs, rigged to the ceiling between two chandeliers. It is an obvious toy prop: hollow moulded plastic, a loose hinged jaw, hands that swing freely. It is NOT a real skeleton, NOT bloody and NOT gory — it is the kind of decoration sold in a shop. Before it drops, the cord and the skeleton are completely out of frame above the ceiling line.

THE SPLIT SCREEN — ONE SURFACE CUT IN FOUR, ABSOLUTELY NO FRAMES
The second half of the film is A FOUR-WAY SPLIT SCREEN that fills the entire 4:3 frame to all four outer edges.
THINK OF IT AS ONE SINGLE PICTURE SLICED BY A VERTICAL LINE AND A HORIZONTAL LINE INTO FOUR EQUAL QUARTERS. The only thing separating the quarters is A SINGLE HAIRLINE SEAM where two pictures meet, as thin as the edge of a cut.
THERE IS NO FRAME, NO BORDER, NO OUTLINE, NO MAT, NO MOUNT, NO CARD, NO WHITE EDGE, NO CREAM EDGE, NO DROP SHADOW, NO BEVEL, NO GUTTER AND NO GAP ANYWHERE. The quarters are NOT photographs, NOT prints, NOT polaroids, NOT cards and NOT windows laid on a background — they are regions of one continuous surface.
EVERY QUARTER HAS SQUARE RIGHT-ANGLED CORNERS. No quarter has rounded corners.
EACH QUARTER'S IMAGE RUNS ALL THE WAY TO ITS OWN EDGES, including the four outer edges of the 4:3 frame.
Quarters that have not arrived yet are FLAT UNTEXTURED SOFT CREAM filling their region completely, also with square corners and no edge treatment.

CROWD RULE — FEW PEOPLE, HELD STEADY
KEEP THE NUMBER OF PEOPLE LOW AND THE CAMERA CLOSE. No shot contains more than FIVE students at once, and most contain two or three. The deep background of the hallway is empty or nearly empty — no rows of tiny distant figures.
EVERY PERSON IN A SHOT KEEPS THE SAME FACE, HAIRSTYLE AND CLOTHES FROM THE FIRST FRAME TO THE LAST. Nobody morphs, swaps identity, changes outfit, appears from nothing or vanishes mid-shot. The count of people in frame stays constant throughout each shot.
Every student in the hallway apart from Enjee is AN ORDINARY ANONYMOUS KOREAN TEENAGER INVENTED FOR THIS SHOT, in plain everyday clothes in muted colours, each with a distinct face. NONE RESEMBLES ANY NAMED CHARACTER — no second Enjee, no turquoise headband or mint jacket like Jenny's, no jewelled clips and fluffy pink cardigan like Olivia's, no glasses and grey sweater like Ryan's, no grey-brown jacket, vest and striped tie like Mark's. No two extras look alike.
NOBODY IN THIS FILM WEARS A MASK OR A COSTUME. Everyone is in ordinary school clothes.
Extras move simply: standing, talking, walking at a steady pace.

WHO HOLDS WHICH COLOUR
ENJEE — PINK. OLIVIA — PINK. JENNY — PALE GREEN. MARK — PALE BLUE. RYAN — PALE BLUE. Extras hold the same handset in assorted pinks, blues and greens.
No real-world phone appears anywhere; the only handset in this film is the one in <<<image_7>>>.

THE SCREEN IN SHOT 6 — A BARE MESSAGE, NOTHING ELSE
The display is a PLAIN FLAT PALE CREAM FIELD filling the whole screen.
At the very top, centred, the sender's name alone in small lowercase letters: chen
Below it, ON THE LEFT-HAND SIDE OF THE SCREEN, ONE SINGLE SOFT PINK ROUNDED BUBBLE, left-aligned, containing exactly these two short lines of plain lowercase sans-serif, both inside that one bubble, on two lines only:
YO EVERYONE
party at my place saturday
THE BUBBLE SITS ON THE LEFT BECAUSE THE MESSAGE IS INCOMING. There is no second bubble and no bubble on the right.
THE REST OF THE SCREEN IS COMPLETELY EMPTY CREAM. There is NO status bar, NO clock, NO battery, NO signal bars, NO wifi symbol, NO back arrow, NO avatar circle, NO app name, NO app icon, NO reply box, NO text field, NO keyboard, NO emoji button, NO plus button, NO attachment icon, NO send button, NO home bar, NO timestamp and NO other writing anywhere.

FORMAT MODE
4:3, 15 seconds, nine timed shots, hard cuts. Normal speed. The first shot is a top-down overhead; every shot after it is at normal eye level.

SHOT 1 (0:00–0:00.9) — overhead
TOP-DOWN OVERHEAD, camera directly above the corridor looking straight down, 63°. The pale marble floor and Enjee fill most of the frame; she walks through from the bottom of the picture, seen from above. ONLY TWO OTHER STUDENTS are in frame, both close to the lens. NOBODY IS HOLDING A PHONE. This is the only overhead shot.

SHOT 2 (0:00.9–0:03.0) — THE PRANK, the hook of the film
Eye level, MEDIUM, 47°, THE CAMERA TRACKING BACKWARD IN FRONT OF HER at her exact walking pace so she stays centred in frame, head to knee. She walks straight toward the lens down the middle of the corridor, bag on her shoulder, both hands empty, looking ahead — relaxed, unhurried. The chandeliers and the pastel wall slide past behind her, soft and out of focus. Nobody is on a phone. THE CEILING ABOVE HER IS EMPTY AND THERE IS NOTHING HANGING IN FRAME.
— 1.4: THE PLASTIC SKELETON DROPS SUDDENLY STRAIGHT DOWN OUT OF THE CEILING on its black cord, falling fast into the top of frame and SNAPPING TO A STOP AT FACE HEIGHT right in front of her, upside down, its skull swinging into her path, arms and jaw flailing from the jolt.
— 1.6: ENJEE JUMPS FOR REAL — shoulders snapping up, a sharp gasp, one hand flying to her chest, a stumbling half step backwards, eyes wide.
— 2.0: The skeleton bounces and swings on the cord, rotating slowly. OFF TO THE SIDE, TWO STUDENTS BURST OUT LAUGHING, one of them doubled over, the other pointing — it was their prank.
— 2.4: She bats the skull aside with the back of her hand and it swings away, half annoyed and half laughing herself.
— 2.8: She blows out a breath, resettles the bag on her shoulder, ducks under the swinging skeleton and keeps walking. Cut.

SHOT 3 (0:03.0–0:04.4) — the ripple, sound first, reaction after
Eye level, MEDIUM, 47°, on THREE STUDENTS at the turquoise lockers, filling the frame from the waist up. Behind them only the lockers and the pastel wall.
They are mid-conversation, hands empty, nobody looking down.
— 3.2 a soft chime sounds; at 3.4 THE BOY ON THE LEFT breaks off and pulls his phone from his jacket.
— 3.7 a low buzz sounds; at 3.9 THE GIRL IN THE MIDDLE goes into her bag.
The third student never checks and keeps talking, mildly annoyed to be ignored.

SHOT 4 (0:04.4–0:06.2) — the shout
Medium, 47°, on TWO BOYS only, one in the foreground with his phone up, the other a few metres behind. Nobody else in frame. The first shouts down the hallway; the second answers while already digging his own phone out of his jacket.

SHOT 5 (0:06.2–0:07.3) — her turn
Medium close-up on Enjee, 47°, from the front, with only soft blurred wall behind her and no other people in frame. She has stopped walking mid-step, head turned toward the voices, HER PHONE STILL IN HER BAG AND BOTH HANDS EMPTY. Then her own sound goes off — the last one in the corridor. Only after it finishes does she reach into her bag and bring the phone out.

SHOT 6 (0:07.3–0:08.6) — the screen, very tight
AN EXTREME CLOSE-UP ON THE SCREEN, 18°, from over her shoulder and slightly above, angled so WE READ IT WITH HER. THE PHONE IS TURNED SCREEN-UP TOWARD HER FACE and HELD ALMOST SQUARE TO THE LENS, tilted no more than five degrees, so THE TEXT SITS HORIZONTALLY LEVEL.
THE DISPLAY FILLS ALMOST THE WHOLE FRAME. Only A NARROW SOFT PINK EDGE of the handset shows down the left and right sides; the top and bottom of the phone are OUTSIDE the frame. Her fingertips curl around the near edge at the bottom corner; her hair falls into the top corner, out of focus. Her thumb rests off the glass, not covering the text.

SHOT 7 (0:08.6–0:09.2) — she just reads
Close-up on Enjee's face, 29°, the screen light soft on her. SHE SIMPLY READS. Her eyes track across the message once. HER FACE DOES NOT CHANGE — no smile, no raised eyebrows, no parted lips, no gasp, no surprise, no delight, no frown. Completely neutral, as if she were checking the time. One ordinary blink. Hard cut on her stillness.

SHOT 8 (0:09.2–0:14.4) — the split screen
Hard cut, with no transition, into the four-way split screen described above — one continuous surface cut into four square-cornered quarters, filling the whole frame, with no frames, borders, mats or gaps of any kind.
Each quarter is a different spot of the same school with its own colour world, shot on grainy 16mm with warm muted tones. EACH QUARTER CONTAINS ONE PERSON ONLY, with no extras behind them.
THE FOUR QUARTERS POP IN ONE AT A TIME, each filling its region exactly as that person starts speaking. Regions not yet arrived are flat cream. Once a quarter arrives it stays. THE LINES RUN BACK TO BACK WITH NO SILENCE BETWEEN THEM, and AFTER SPEAKING EVERY PERSON KEEPS MOVING AND KEEPS ACTING — nobody freezes. EACH CHARACTER SAYS ONLY THEIR OWN LINE, ONCE.
— 0:09.2, TOP-LEFT arrives, OLIVIA: sitting on the window bench under the arched window, pink handset in both hands, knees bouncing. She snaps her head up into the lens and speaks. AFTER HER LINE she squeals silently, kicks her feet, drops her head back down and types fast with both thumbs, grinning.
— 0:10.5, TOP-RIGHT arrives, MARK: in front of the turquoise lockers in his grey-brown jacket, blue handset in one hand, already in motion. He speaks into the lens. AFTER HIS LINE he keeps going — pushes off the lockers, throws a loose shoulder-roll, points at someone off-frame, bounces on his toes, pockets the phone and shadow-boxes a lazy punch. He never stops moving.
— 0:11.9, BOTTOM-LEFT arrives, JENNY: beside a gold baroque mirror, green handset in one hand, her reflection visible. Her eyes go phone, mirror, phone. She speaks. AFTER HER LINE she turns side-on to the mirror, pulls her jacket open and closed, lifts her hair off her neck and frowns at herself.
— 0:13.1, BOTTOM-RIGHT arrives, RYAN: walking slowly between two pink columns with A STACK OF THREE OR FOUR BOOKS HELD AGAINST HIS HIP IN ONE ARM and the blue handset in his other hand, reading it as he goes. He is NOT posed for the camera and does not look into the lens. He slows, reads, and speaks half to himself. AFTER HIS LINE he shifts the books higher, pockets the phone, and KEEPS WALKING STRAIGHT OUT OF HIS QUARTER, leaving it empty.

SHOT 9 (0:14.4–0:15) — transition
The whole split screen whips hard to the right in a fast motion-blurred slide and exits frame; the final frame is a streaked blur.

ACTING TASKS (each fully invested in a tactic; the work happens in the eyes)
SCENE DIRECTION (shared, unspoken): Chen's invite just dropped, and everyone works out in one second what this party means for them.
ENJEE (the prank) — the jump is involuntary and genuine, a real startle before her brain catches up; a beat later she sees what it is, and the annoyance that arrives is already half amused by the time she swats it away. She is not frightened afterwards and does not run.
THE TWO LAUGHING STUDENTS — they rigged it and they are thrilled it worked. Pure delighted schoolboy laughter, nothing mean in it.
ENJEE — MOTIVE: she never expected Chen to invite her. GOAL: find out whether this is real before she lets herself feel anything. TACTIC: in shot 2 she is thinking about nothing at all; in shot 7 she reads it flat, giving nothing away.
OLIVIA — MOTIVE: she lives for this. GOAL: be the first one in. TACTIC: declares it into the lens and is already replying.
MARK — MOTIVE: parties are his stage. GOAL: get everybody hyped. TACTIC: pitches it into the lens, then performs for whoever is nearby.
JENNY — MOTIVE: Chen will see her there. GOAL: the perfect look. OBSTACLE: nothing she owns feels good enough. TACTIC: judges her reflection like a rival.
RYAN — MOTIVE: Enjee will be there, which he would never say out loud. GOAL: find a way to go. OBSTACLE: Saturday belongs to his family. TACTIC: rereads the date while walking; the smile dies on the word.
EXTRAS — before their sound they are mid-conversation and not thinking about phones; after it they look down and show each other screens.
(Safety: gaze always engaged in the task — never a frozen, glassy, unfocused stare; natural blink cadence.)

PHYSICS
The skeleton falls under real gravity, accelerating, then the cord goes taut and snaps it to a stop so the limbs and jaw whip out and keep swinging and rotating afterwards; it is light hollow plastic and it knocks and rattles. Enjee's whole body reacts to the startle — weight back onto the heel, bag swinging on her shoulder, hair lifting and settling. Footsteps on marble with real contact.

LIGHTING
Soft morning daylight from the arched window at the far end, warm glow from the chandeliers, gentle bounce off the pastel walls; eyes readable throughout. In shot 6 the screen is evenly lit with no glare across the text. In the split screen each quarter keeps its own motivated light: warm window light for Olivia, cool turquoise for Mark, amber mirror glow for Jenny, dusty pink for Ryan.

AUDIO
Hallway ambience: footsteps on marble with a little room echo, chatter and laughter carrying from off-frame, a locker door.
1.4 — a quick whoosh and a dry plastic rattle as the skeleton drops and the cord snaps taut.
1.6 — Enjee's sharp involuntary gasp.
1.9 — two boys cracking up off to the side, delighted.
THE NOTIFICATION SOUNDS ARE ALL DIFFERENT AND ARRIVE SEPARATELY, EACH LANDING BEFORE ITS OWN STUDENT MOVES:
3.2 — a soft two-note chime.
3.7 — a low double buzz.
4.2 — a bright single ping, off-frame.
4.8 — a short marimba tone, off-frame.
7.4 — one more, soft and close: Enjee's own.
No two overlap and no two sound alike.
5.0 — BOY, shouting down the hallway: "Yo, Chen's throwing a Halloween party!"
5.9 — SECOND BOY, pulling out his own phone: "No way, for real?"
In the split screen, a soft pop on each quarter's arrival, then the four lines back to back with no gaps:
9.4 — OLIVIA: "Oh my God, I'm so going."
10.6 — MARK: "Bro, this is gonna be insane."
12.0 — JENNY: "Ugh, I have nothing to wear."
13.2 — RYAN, half to himself as he walks: "...Of course it's Saturday."
14.4 — a sharp whoosh on the whip.
All six lines are native, casual American teenage English, clearly articulated, at an ordinary conversational rate. ENJEE NEVER SPEAKS. No music. No subtitles. No narration.

STYLE
Hallway: bright, airy pastel K-drama look, glossy and clean, fine grain. Split screen: 16mm grain and a warm muted grade inside each quarter, deadpan indie music-video feel. The grain and grade live INSIDE the picture, never as an edge treatment.

QUALITY
Sharp clarity, stable picture, natural colours, readable faces, controlled highlights; natural motion blur only on the falling skeleton and during the whip.
EVERY PERSON IS ANATOMICALLY CORRECT AND TEMPORALLY STABLE — faces hold their features for the whole shot, hands have five fingers, limbs stay attached and correctly proportioned, clothing keeps its colour and cut, and nobody warps, melts, duplicates or flickers.
THE TEXT ON THE SCREEN IN SHOT 6 IS CRISP, HORIZONTALLY LEVEL AND PERFECTLY LEGIBLE, reading exactly "YO EVERYONE" on the first line and "party at my place saturday" on the second, both inside the one bubble, never spilling onto a third line. No ghosting, no flicker.

POSITIVE CONSTRAINTS
THE FILM OPENS WITH THE PRANK: within the first two seconds, a plastic Halloween skeleton drops out of the ceiling on a cord straight into Enjee's face and she visibly jumps. This is the hook and it must land hard.
THE SKELETON IS AN OBVIOUS CHEAP PLASTIC DECORATION hanging on a thin black cord — hollow, bone-white, with a loose hinged jaw. It is not a real skeleton and there is nothing gory about it.
THE CEILING IS EMPTY UNTIL THE DROP — nothing hangs in frame before 1.4 seconds.
AFTER THE SCARE ENJEE SWATS IT ASIDE AND SIMPLY WALKS ON. She is calm again by the next shot.
NOBODY IN THIS FILM WEARS A MASK OR A COSTUME. There is no horse mask and no masked person anywhere.
THE SPLIT SCREEN HAS NO FRAMES, NO BORDERS, NO OUTLINES, NO MATS, NO WHITE OR CREAM EDGES, NO DROP SHADOWS, NO BEVELS, NO GUTTERS AND NO GAPS. The quarters meet on a hairline seam and all four fill the frame to its outer edges.
EVERY QUARTER HAS SQUARE RIGHT-ANGLED CORNERS — none are rounded.
THE QUARTERS ARE NOT PHOTOGRAPHS, CARDS, PRINTS, POLAROIDS OR WINDOWS ON A BACKGROUND. They are regions of one continuous surface.
ENJEE IS SEEN WALKING AT EYE LEVEL IN SHOT 2, tracked from the front, before anything happens.
NO SHOT CONTAINS MORE THAN FIVE PEOPLE. The camera stays close and the deep background is empty.

ACTING TASK (each character is fully invested in a tactic; the work happens in the eyes)
SCENE DIRECTION (shared, unspoken): keep it light — tonight is supposed to be fun.
CHEN — MOTIVE: he wants one particular guest to walk into a perfect night. TACTIC: he checks every detail with his eyes, adjusts it, checks again — the house first, then himself.
MARK — MOTIVE: none at all; he was ready an hour ago and has been waiting. TACTIC: conserves energy, does the minimum, enjoys watching Chen fuss. His line is not a joke — he genuinely has been ready this whole time and is mildly relieved it's finally over.
JENNY — MOTIVE: tonight she must be the one everyone looks at. TACTIC: she judges each dress against her reflection hunting for "the one", and runs out of patience fast.
ENJEE (montage) — MOTIVE: she wants to belong at this party. TACTIC: she weighs each option seriously, comparing them as if one wrong choice would prove she doesn't fit in.
ENJEE (call) — GOAL: get Ryan to say yes without sounding like she needs him there. OBSTACLE: if she pushes, he will hear how nervous she is. TACTIC: she asks casually and listens hard for any hesitation in his voice.
— "Hey — you're coming to Chen's party tonight, right?" — her eyes already expect a yes.
— (listening) — eyes hunting for any way he might still come.
— "Oh... okay. No, it's fine." — she lets him off the hook to protect him; her eyes drop to the hat only after she has said it.
— "Yeah. ...You too." — the line breaks after "Yeah."

SCENE CONTEXT
Night, the bench outside the dormitory. Enjee is still working on the graze on Ryan's cheek with a cotton bud, holding his jaw steady with her other hand. He apologises WHILE she works — two short sentences, one straight after the other, for keeping the truth about his family from her — and it costs him: he is ashamed, his head moves in a small slow shake at himself as he says it, and his voice thickens. She does not stop; she keeps treating the wound and keeps glancing up from it to his eyes. She gives the graze one last touch, takes both hands away from his face, looks at him and answers in one flat sentence. He nods. A short beat. Then the corner of her mouth goes and she adds a condition that lets them both out of it — and he raises it, completely straight-faced. Eighteen seconds, one location, eleven timed shots. Voices and sound effects only; no music.

SPEECH RATE — THE MOST IMPORTANT RULE IN THIS FILM
There are only five short lines in eighteen seconds, and each one has been given more time than it needs. EVERY WORD IS FULLY PRONOUNCED AT A CALM, DELIBERATE, CONVERSATIONAL SPEAKING RATE — roughly three to four syllables per second, the pace of someone speaking carefully to one person sitting close to them. Every syllable is audible and every word is clearly articulated.
Approximate length of each line as spoken:
— "I'm sorry I hid the truth about my family." takes ABOUT THREE AND A HALF SECONDS.
— "It was wrong." takes ABOUT ONE SECOND.
— "Okay. Just don't hide things from me again." takes ABOUT THREE SECONDS.
— "And you're buying me lunch. For a week." takes ABOUT TWO AND A HALF SECONDS.
— "Two weeks." takes ABOUT ONE SECOND.
NO LINE IS EVER COMPRESSED, SPED UP, CLIPPED OR SQUEEZED TO FIT. If a line needs a moment more, the silence around it gives way — the words never do. Nobody gabbles, nobody rushes, nobody swallows the ends of words.

EMOTION SLOWS HIM DOWN, IT DOES NOT SPEED HIM UP
Ryan is emotional and guilty when he apologises — and guilt makes a person speak MORE SLOWLY, not faster. The feeling weighs his words down. His voice is low and a little thick, the breath is not quite steady, and each word comes out heavier and slower than his normal speech. He is not agitated and he is not in a hurry to get it over with.

HIS HEAD MOVES WHILE HE SPEAKS — GUILT
As he says the apology he gives A SMALL, SLOW SHAKE OF THE HEAD — a few degrees left and right, twice, aimed at himself, the way someone does when they cannot believe what they did. His eyes drop from hers for a moment on the shake and come back up. His jaw is tight, his throat works once before he starts, and his eyebrows pull slightly together in the middle. Because Enjee's hand is under his jaw, HER HAND MOVES WITH HIM and then steadies him again — she adjusts her grip a fraction to keep the bud on the wound. The head movement is small and controlled, never a big theatrical swing.

ENJEE'S SKIN IS PERFECTLY CLEAR
Enjee's complexion is ONE SMOOTH EVEN TONE from hairline to jaw and down the neck — uniform, unbroken, healthy, flawless. Both of her cheeks are exactly the same clean colour as her forehead and her chin: smooth, matte, untouched skin all the way across. Her hands are clean. The ointment, the shine and the injury belong to Ryan's right cheekbone alone and appear nowhere else in the film.

RYAN'S CARDIGAN IS CLEAN
The pale blue ribbed cardigan is ONE EVEN, UNIFORM PALE BLUE across the entire garment — left shoulder, right shoulder, both sleeves, chest and back are all exactly the same fresh clean shade, as if it came straight out of the wardrobe. The white shirt collar and cuffs are crisp white. The wool colour is continuous and consistent everywhere.

RYAN'S TWO SENTENCES RUN STRAIGHT ON
His apology is two sentences said one after the other as a single continuous thought. BETWEEN THEM THERE IS ONLY A BREATH — under half a second. He does not stop, does not search for the words and does not sit thinking between the two lines. He already knows what he is going to say; he says it, and then he stops.

Night, the bench outside the dormitory. The film opens on a short whip-pan camera move, then settles. Enjee is already working on the graze on Ryan's cheek with a cotton bud, holding his jaw steady with her other hand. He apologises WHILE she works — two short sentences, one straight after the other, for keeping the truth about his family from her — and it costs him: he is ashamed, his head moves in a small slow shake at himself as he says it, and his voice thickens. She does not stop; she keeps treating the wound and keeps glancing up from it to his eyes. She gives the graze one last touch, takes both hands away from his face, looks at him and answers in one flat sentence. He nods. A short beat. Then the corner of her mouth goes and she adds a condition that lets them both out of it — and he raises it, completely straight-faced. Eighteen seconds, one location, eleven timed shots. The opening is three beats and no more — the pencil, the corner, and straight into her head. The last three and a half seconds are a held tail so the piece does not end abruptly. Voice and sound effects only — no music track. THREE voices are heard inside Jenny's head — the remembered principal, the remembered mother, and Jenny's own interior voice. None is narration and no new scene is shown for any of them.

THE FRIENDS NEVER STOP — A RULE FOR THE WHOLE PART
The two friends are having an ordinary, continuous, animated conversation with each other from the first second to the last. They talk over each other, gesture, laugh, lean in, shift their weight. THEY DO NOT STOP TALKING AT ANY POINT, THEY DO NOT FALL SILENT, THEY DO NOT FREEZE, AND THEY DO NOT TURN AND STARE AT JENNY. In every shot where either is in frame they are visibly mid-conversation and moving. Their voices are continuously present on the track the whole way through, including underneath the remembered conversation and underneath Jenny's interior voice; they only drop in level, never to silence, and they are never intelligible. The single exception is friend one breaking off for her one line near the end, after which she turns straight back and carries on.

HOW JENNY PLAYS IT — EXPRESSION NOTES ONLY
SHE IS SIMPLY SITTING THERE. No pretend smile, no nodding along, no laughing, no reacting to the story at any point. Her face is quiet and unarranged, her eyes unfocused, plainly occupied with something that is not in this room.
SHE NEVER FREEZES. Going inward is active: her head drifts a few degrees and comes back, tips slightly at her own inner question, her chin lowers a fraction, she swallows, her breath moves, her brows work. Never a statue, never a blank motionless stare.
SHE SQUINTS SLIGHTLY while the two remembered voices play — brows drawing together, eyes narrowing — the look of someone who heard the words through a door perfectly well and still cannot work out what those two adults meant by them.
SHE SAYS NOTHING OUT LOUD UNTIL THE LAST EXCHANGE. Her question is thought, not spoken: HER LIPS DO NOT MOVE, she does not mouth it, does not whisper it, and her jaw stays closed.
THE ONLY SMILE IN THE SCENE IS THE FALSE ONE NEAR THE END, on for less than a second and gone again.

1.6–4.2 — Shot 2, the three-shot of the front-left corner. Friend two mid-story with her hands, friend one answering and laughing, both animated — and Jenny between them with her books, face quiet, eyes unfocused, giving them nothing, the pencil still going in her hand. Across this shot the friends' voices begin to recede, as if the room were getting longer, with a low hum rising under them.
4.2–9.6 — Shot 3, close on Jenny, the tapping continuing underneath. THE REMEMBERED CONVERSATION COMES UP ALMOST AT ONCE, and it is two people: first the principal, a man's voice, low, close to the door; then a pause; then her mother answering him, sharper and final. Her head angles a few degrees toward her left, the way you turn an ear at something you are trying to hear properly; her chin lowers; she swallows once; and as her mother's answer runs she begins to squint, brows drawing together. 9.6–10.8 — Shot 4, the pencil, her mother's line finishing over it, the yellow catching the window light.
10.8–13.4 — Shot 5, her face. The remembered voices stop and she turns the exchange over: the squint deepens, the head tips a fraction the other way, her lips press together. 13.4–14.6 — Shot 6, the pencil. Two more taps; then it STOPS, dead.
14.6–20.0 — Shot 7, the medium, slowly pushing in. HER OWN VOICE GOES THROUGH HER HEAD — the question, then the second one, then the flat impossible fact — and SHE DOES NOT SPEAK. Friend one, in the middle of saying something to friend two, breaks off mid-sentence, turns, leans across and PUTS A HAND ON JENNY'S SHOULDER — and the room's sound comes straight back to normal volume with the touch. ACTING TASK — JENNY (fully invested in her tactic; the work happens in her eyes)
SCENE DIRECTION (shared with the friends, unspoken): break time, three girls, a story.
MOTIVE (her fuel): yesterday she stood outside a door and heard the principal ask her mother how she had been, in the voice of a man who already knew her — and heard her mother shut it down with a sentence that had twenty years inside it. She has not slept.
GOAL: make that exchange fit something she already knows.
OBSTACLE: it does not fit anything, and every time she tries, the room goes further away.
TACTIC: she has stopped bothering to keep up with the conversation at all — she just sits in it and works the problem with her eyes, replaying the door, replaying both voices and the tone between them, hunting the memory for a man she might have missed. The questions never leave her mouth; it all runs inside and only the face shows the working. When the hand lands on her shoulder she is genuinely interrupted, and she does the minimum required to be left alone: the fast yes, the fast smile — and the second the friend turns away she stops paying for it and goes back down.
Moment to moment:
— the pencil at the top — she does not know she is doing it.
— the corner — nothing from her; she sits, eyes elsewhere, while the two of them talk.
— the principal's voice — the head angles toward it like an ear at a door; it is the FAMILIARITY in it she is listening to, not the words.
— her mother's answer — the squint starts; that sentence is the part that will not go anywhere.
— the eyes flicking left — toward a door that is not there.
— the pencil stopping — the thought lands.
— "Were they… acquainted before?" — thought, not said; the brows lift a fraction; the mouth does not move.
— "But how?" — thought; the eyes search fast through years; the mouth does not move.
— "I've never seen a man around my mom since I was born." — thought; the smallest not-quite-shake of the head; the breath goes out; the mouth does not move.
— the held close — still inside it; the puzzlement is not resolving.
— the hand on her shoulder — a real interruption; a beat of not having heard; then the reflex.
— "Yeah— yeah, I'm okay." — too quick, the smile switched on and off like a light; the eyes never join in.
— the tail — the mask comes off the instant she is not being looked at; the eyes go down; the same face returns; the pencil starts again.
(Safety: she is thinking, not vacant — gaze always engaged in the task, never a frozen glassy stare, never motionless; natural blink cadence.)

THE FRIENDS — alive, animated and unaware for the entire part: friend two tells a story with her hands from the desk in front, friend one answers, laughs and interrupts from the desk beside. They talk to each other across Jenny without pause, without going quiet and without turning to look at her — until the single moment at 22.8 when friend one breaks off mid-sentence, touches Jenny's shoulder and asks her one line. She takes the answer at face value and turns straight back to friend two, continuing through the whole tail. None of their other words is intelligible.

ACTING TASK — RYAN (fully invested in his tactic; the work happens in his eyes)
SCENE DIRECTION (shared, unspoken): get her to stop before the door.
MOTIVE (his fuel): if she goes through that door without hearing him, the version of him she carries in there is the liar, and that version sets.
GOAL: one sentence before the door.
OBSTACLE: the floor, and then the door.
TACTIC: from the floor he does not try to get up first — he shouts first, because the door is closer than his feet are. He watches off-frame for the turn that does not come, and when
the door slams his eyes stay on it for a full second before they drop.
Moment to moment:
— the trip — he is looking at her off-frame, not at the floor, which is why he falls.
— the landing — real winded shock, and then he immediately discards it; the pain never becomes the subject.
— "Enjee, wait…" — thrown from the floor past the lens, all breath.
— "…let me explain…" — quieter; he already knows, off-frame, that her hand is on the door.
(Safety: gaze always engaged in the task — never a frozen, glassy stare; natural blink cadence.)

— the walk to the door — her shoulders are up and locked; she is holding something in with her whole upper body.
— the hand on the handle — no hesitation, because hesitating would be visible from behind.
— on the sill — comfortable, unguarded, sitting the way you sit with people you trust.
— the laugh — full and real, given to the friend who earned it.
— the turn over her shoulder — pulled, not chosen. The body stays where it is; only the head goes.
— looking down through the glass — reading the red jacket, then the bike, then confirming the hair; the mouth stays open from the laugh.

the polished stone before settling on his hip; the glasses shift crooked on his nose and stay crooked; the cardigan bunches. Enjee's walk is fast and even with her platform sandals
flat on the marble, the backpack riding on her shoulders, her hair swinging behind her; the door handle turns with real resistance under her hand. The bathroom door is a solid panel
on a closer: it swings fast, slams flat, and the handle rattles once.
In the classroom: the stone sill takes her weight solidly and does not move; her laugh rocks her shoulders and her free foot swings slightly; her hair swings forward and settles; the
skirt ruffles shift on the stone. The turn over her shoulder is a real neck-and-shoulder rotation with the hair carrying a short delay, and her seated body stays put.
In the courtyard: Chen's steps land with real weight on dry stone, the cropped red jacket moves with his stride and settles when he stops, and the helmet has real mass as he lifts it
off the seat and lets his arm hang with it. THE BIKE DOES NOT MOVE AT ALL — it stays upright on its side-stand, the suspension does not settle, the stand does not fold, nothing
rocks. The paving is dry and flat.

Three shots, 15 seconds total. Shot 1 is one continuous 8-second point-of-view shot running at roughly 70% speed — slowed, heavy and dreamlike, but still moving enough to carry
him the whole way in. Shot 2 is a 2-second top-down shot at 100% speed. Shot 3 is a 5-second side shot at 100% speed. Hard cut at 08.0 s and hard cut at 10.0 s. No dissolves
anywhere.

OPTICS
Shot 1: 84° diagonal field of view at her eye height, classic wide rectilinear character — the natural span of human sight, wide enough for the corridor walls to fall away at the
edges and for him to fill the frame as he closes in. Lens locked for the whole eight seconds; he grows in frame only because he gets closer. Focus is deliberately soft and shallow
for the entire dream: the corridor, the lockers, the mirrors and the far end all sit in creamy defocus, and he is the only thing that resolves — from 02.0 onward his face and eyes
carry clean readable focus inside an otherwise soft picture.
Shot 2: 63° looking straight down from 2.4 m above the mattress, lens locked — wide enough to hold her whole sprawled body and the wrecked bedding around her, close enough that
her face and her wide-open eyes are clearly readable. Focus sharp edge to edge.
Shot 3: 47° at 1.8 m from the side of the bed, lens locked for the whole five seconds — a medium shot that holds her from the hips up while she sits, close enough that her face,
her eyes and her hands in her hair all read clearly. Focus sharp edge to edge.

CAMERA
Setup A — HER EYES. Camera at 1.6 m in the middle of the corridor facing straight down its length, behaving exactly as described in THE CAMERA IS HER EYES. It never travels
forward and never pushes in. Its only translation is BACKWARD, in her three retreating steps.
Setup B — TOP-DOWN. Camera directly above the bed, about 2.4 m up, aimed straight down at the centre of the mattress with the long side of the bed running across the frame,
static and level. It sees her sprawled diagonally below it with the twisted duvet, the bare mattress corner, the throw and the pillow on the floor spread out around her, and she
is staring straight up into it. Locked off for the whole two seconds.
Setup C — SIDE, MATTRESS HEIGHT. Camera 0.7 m high, 1.8 m out from the long side of the bed, level with the mattress and aimed straight across it, static. It holds her from the
hips up as she sits in the middle of the wrecked bed, wide enough to keep the twisted duvet and the bare mattress corner in frame, close enough that her face, her eyes and both
hands in her hair are clearly readable. Locked off for the whole five seconds — no push-in, no drift, no reframe.

ACTION TIMING (15 s)
[00.0-08.0] SHOT 1 — Setup A. ONE CONTINUOUS POINT-OF-VIEW SHOT. No cuts and no interruptions. Everything is soft, and everything echoes.
00.0-00.9 the empty corridor, thick with mist and drifting glints of light, beams lying across the air, the whole picture softly diffused and glowing. The frame sways gently with
her breathing. Five metres ahead the door in the left-hand wall is already swinging open and a huge slow billow of white steam rolls out into the corridor and spreads.
00.9-02.0 he steps out of the doorway inside the steam and turns into the centre of the corridor, already walking toward the lens. Backlit by the far windows, he reads as a soft
dark shape in a white glow, with a rim of light along the shoulders and the wet hair. No face yet. She thinks nothing in words — she simply keeps looking, and the frame stays on
him and breathes.
02.0-02.6 he crosses into the hard beam from the windows and HIS FACE BECOMES CLEARLY READABLE — the first thing in the whole dream to come properly into focus: wet slicked-back
hair, water beading on his skin, and his eyes already locked on the lens. Everything around him stays soft.
02.0 THE MOVE BEGINS AND NEVER STOPS. From this moment he does not pause, does not slow and does not stop again for the rest of the shot. He simply keeps coming.
02.6-03.6 ENJU, INTERNAL VOICE, HER ONLY LINE IN THE WHOLE SEGMENT, softly, amazed, half a laugh in it and completely baffled: "Oh... Ryan?" After this she is silent for the rest
of the dream, and everything else she feels is played in where she looks and how much corridor she gives up.
03.4-04.3 she gives ground: the frame pushes BACKWARD one step with a small bounce as her weight lands, then holds and breathes. He closes the distance again immediately, so the
gap never really grows.
04.3-05.3 a second backward step, shorter than the first, and he gains on it. He is filling more of the frame every time she looks. Water on his skin and in his hair catches the
beams and blooms into soft points of light. The mist parts around his legs and closes behind him.
05.3-06.2 a third step, the shortest of the three. He gains again. He is more than half the frame now, and nothing about him has changed: same pace, same line, same eyes, and the
fact that nothing changes is what makes it land.
06.2-06.8 the corridor runs out behind her. The frame stops moving backward and settles, breathing. He keeps coming.
06.8-07.0 he takes the last step in and comes right into her space, filling the frame from the chest up.
07.0-07.4 RYAN, low and easy, almost private, close to the lens: "Hey."
07.4-08.0 HE GOES TO KISS HER. He leans in without stopping, his face coming closer and growing in frame, angled down at her because he is above her and close. NOTHING TOUCHES
HER — no hand comes into frame, he never reaches out, and his hands stay exactly where they are. As he leans, THE WHOLE FRAME TILTS UP five to seven degrees, slowly and smoothly,
and stays there: her own head tipping back to hold his face. His eyes hold the lens until the last moment and then soften. Everything in the frame says the kiss is about to
happen — and NOTHING HAPPENS. Before he arrives it all breaks: an alarm cuts in at about 07.5, the light pulses hard, the white mist floods in from every edge and swallows the
frame, the chandeliers smear into soft haloes, his face is the last readable thing in the white and then it is gone too.
[08.0-10.0] SHOT 2 — HARD CUT to Setup B, TOP-DOWN from directly above the bed, 100% speed, dry sound, clean and sharp with all the mist, glow, softness and echo gone. Locked off.
Seen from straight above, Enju lies sprawled diagonally across the bed, her head near the corner of the mattress, one arm flung out above her head and the other trapped under her.
Her long hair is a complete mess, knotted across the sheet and half over her face. The dusty pink duvet is shoved down and twisted around one leg and hanging off the side; the
green knitted throw is on the floor; her pillow is off the bed entirely. Her sleep mask has slipped up onto her forehead at an angle. The alarm is loud and close in the room.
08.0-08.4 SHE WAKES WITH A JOLT AND SHE WAKES FRIGHTENED — her whole body flinches once, hard: her shoulders come up off the mattress, her outstretched arm snatches in toward her,
her leg kicks free of the duvet, and her eyes snap open wide, staring straight up into the lens above her. One sharp involuntary intake of breath through the mouth.
08.4-10.0 she does not move again. She blinks twice, hard and fast. Her eyes dart once left and once right without her head moving, reading the ceiling and the room for where she
is. She is completely disoriented, her eyes are wide and startled, and her breathing is fast and audible through her mouth.
[10.0-15.0] SHOT 3 — HARD CUT to Setup C, from the side of the bed at mattress height, 100% speed, locked off. This shot carries her all the way to the end.
10.0-10.9 she bolts upright in one abrupt uncoordinated movement and ends up sitting in the middle of the wrecked bed, hair everywhere, mask crooked on her head, breathing hard.
10.9-12.6 IT BREAKS OUT OF HER. Both hands fly up into her hair and grab two fistfuls at the sides of her head, and she SHAKES HER HEAD hard from side to side and lets out one
loud frustrated shout — a single burst of flustered, embarrassed disbelief, not fear and not distress. Her whole upper body rocks with it, her hair whips and settles late, her
elbows are up and out, and her eyes are squeezed shut for the length of the shout.
12.6-13.4 it drains straight back out of her. The shout stops, her head stops moving, her hands loosen in her hair, and her eyes open again. She is breathing hard through her
mouth and looking at nothing.
13.4-15.0 she goes completely still and stays sitting there, THINKING — trying to work out what that even was. Her hands slide slowly down out of her hair and one of them settles
on the top of her own head and stays. She stares straight ahead at nothing, her eyes lose focus and come back once, and her breathing slowly steadies. The alarm keeps going and
she does not turn it off. The shot does not end on a movement: the frame simply holds on her sitting there and thinking, calm and unresolved, until the last frame.

THE EVENT OF THE SCENE — being wanted, and having it confiscated. Everything in these fifteen seconds is one process: a question asked in a dream and unanswered on waking. The
end of the segment is not a punchline and not a reaction — it is her sitting in the wreckage of her own bed with her own hand on her own head, still asking.
SCENE DIRECTION (shared, unspoken, played by both): in the dream, do not break the spell — behave as though all of this were completely normal.
THE PHYSICAL CHANNEL. The terrain is a corridor and a bed. Each of them pursues the event through his or her own visible behaviour: ENJU through LOOKING AND GIVING GROUND in the
dream — she has no body there and almost no words, so all of her doing is where her eyes go and how much corridor she surrenders — and then through HER OWN BODY awake, in the
jolt, the hands in her hair and the stillness at the end. RYAN through ADVANCING — one unbroken approach that never pauses, never slows and never asks.
THE CONTRAST. Enju is UNCHOSEN but awake to it; Ryan is UNREAL but completely certain. The essential axis the audience reads is whether being wanted is real — she is the one who
doubts it, he is the one who never has.

ACTING TASK — ENJU
MOTIVE (her fuel): nothing this good has ever been aimed at her, and some part of her already knows it cannot be real — which is exactly why she will not look away.
GOAL: find out whether this is being aimed at her, and survive being looked at while she works it out.
OBSTACLE: he will not stop coming, there is barely a metre and a half of corridor behind her, and then her own alarm clock takes the whole thing away.
TACTIC IN THE DREAM: she looks, and the looking is slow, and she barely says anything — the amazement stays inside her. She does not recognise him through the steam, so she waits
rather than searches. The moment his face resolves she stops assessing him and starts quietly failing to understand. Then she does the only thing a body does when something
impossible walks at it: she gives ground, without deciding to and without looking behind her. She is not fleeing and she is not frightened; she is making room she does not have.
When the corridor runs out she stops, and stopping is not a decision — it is simply the end of the retreat. When he arrives in her space she stays completely still, because moving
might end it.
TACTIC AWAKE: the fright comes first and it is pure body — she is startled out of somewhere, not scared of anything in the room. Then, the moment she works out that it was a
dream, the whole thing lands on her at once and she throws it out of herself in one loud burst with both hands in her hair. And then it is gone and there is nothing left to do
with it, so she sits and tries to understand what her own head just did to her.
Moment to moment:
— the first second — silence and stillness; she is not searching, she is just looking at an empty corridor full of light
— the steam and the figure — pure wordless curiosity, no fear and no excitement
— the face resolving — she stops being curious and starts being lost
— "Oh... Ryan?" — her one and only line, and all of her amazement is in it: astonishment and confusion arriving together, said calmly, with half a laugh she does not finish
— the three steps back — the first is involuntary, the second and third are real recalculations, and each is shorter than the last
— the wall behind her — she runs out and stops, and there is nothing behind her
— him arriving in her space — she stays completely still: she does not back away further, does not brace and does not look away
— her head tipping back — her own small movement to keep his face in view; she is not helping anything and not resisting anything
— him going to kiss her — she stops breathing and stops thinking; she is not anticipating and not deciding, she is simply not moving
— the jolt, seen from above — the body goes before the mind; the eyes open as part of the flinch, not after it, and they are frightened for exactly as long as it takes her to
recognise her own ceiling
— the seconds after — she reads the room for where she is before she reads herself for what happened
— sitting up — abrupt and uncoordinated, no grace in it at all
— the hands in the hair and the shout — flustered, embarrassed, exasperated disbelief thrown out in one burst; it is the sound of someone who cannot believe her own brain, not
the sound of someone in trouble
— the drop — it empties out of her as fast as it arrived and leaves her with nothing
— the last beat — she is not remembering and not enjoying it; she is checking, and she does not reach an answer before the segment ends
(Safety: her eyes are dry throughout — she is startled and flustered, never upset, never crying and never in distress. Her gaze is always engaged in a real task, never a frozen
glassy stare; natural uneven blink cadence. Her single internal line in the dream is never lip-synced and her mouth does not move to it.)

ACTING TASK — RYAN (fully invested in his tactic; the work happens in his eyes)
MOTIVE (his fuel): in her dream he has never once doubted anything, least of all whether she wants him to walk over.
GOAL: close the distance, and keep closing it.
OBSTACLE: none, and the total absence of hesitation is what makes him magnetic.
TACTIC: he refuses to hurry and refuses to look anywhere else. He found her before we could see his face, and from then on he keeps her, holding her eyes the whole way in and
reading her the entire time — watching what she does with being looked at and with being walked at. He does not react to her giving ground, does not acknowledge it and does not
slow for it; he simply takes back whatever she gives up. He does not stop and wait at any point, because stopping would be a question and he has none. Then he comes the last of
the way in and goes to kiss her, and he never once reaches for her.
Moment to moment:
— stepping out of the doorway — no pause and no entrance; he continues into the corridor as if he had planned to
— the approach — he keeps her and gives up nothing; the walk itself is the whole tactic
— the moment his face resolves in the beam — his eyes are already on her; nothing about him has to change, and that is the effect
— each step she retreats — he answers it without registering it, and gains a little
— arriving — one continuous movement into her space, no stopping and no waiting
— "Hey." — low and easy, thrown into the middle of his own movement, and he watches it land
— going in for the kiss — the same tempo as everything else; his hands stay exactly where they are, he never reaches out and never touches her, he is not rushing to it and he
never gets there
(Safety: eyes wide open with the full iris and a bright catchlight visible, never half-shut, drooping or squinting; steady unbroken eye contact with the lens from the moment his
face is readable; natural blink cadence. He never looks down at his own body, never adjusts the towel for effect and never breaks his own rhythm.)

BACKGROUND
There is no background action and there are no other people. The corridor is empty of everyone except Ryan for the entire dream — no students, no figures, no silhouettes, no
shapes, nobody in the distance, nobody at the frame edges and nobody passing the lens at any point. The only things moving in shot 1 are him, the mist, the light and the water.
In shots 2 and 3 Enju is alone in the bedroom and nobody else appears.

DREAM LOOK — SHOT 1 ONLY
The corridor is already a dream in the very first frame. Nothing "becomes" dreamlike — it starts that way and stays. This is a good dream: warm, soft, kind and magical, never
eerie and never cold.
THE DREAMY BLUR. The whole dream image is gently out of focus in a soft, pleasant, magical way — a light optical diffusion laid over everything, the way a dream remembers a place
rather than records it. Focus is shallow and soft everywhere: the corridor, the lockers, the gilded mirrors, the chandeliers and the far end all sit in creamy defocus with soft
round out-of-focus highlights, and only he resolves — from 02.0 onward his face and his eyes are the one clean, readable, properly focused thing in the frame. The edges and
corners of the picture are softer than the centre, and the softness increases with distance until the far end of the corridor is nothing but glowing white. Highlights bleed
gently into whatever surrounds them, contrast is low and creamy, and skin, water and mist all read velvety. This is real optical softness — genuine diffusion and shallow depth of
field — steady and even for all eight seconds, never smear, never doubled edges, never ghosting and never digital blur.
THE MIST. Thick white mist fills the corridor from floor to ceiling, denser with distance until the far end is nothing but pale glowing white. A heavier layer lies along the floor
and rolls slowly. It never clears.
THE STEAM. The plain door releases a heavy, slow, rolling cloud of white steam that pours out at floor level, billows to head height and feeds into the mist. He walks out of that
cloud and it keeps trailing off his shoulders and his wet hair for the whole shot.
THE LIGHT IN THE AIR. Because the air is thick, every light source is visible as volume: wide soft shafts fall from the arched windows behind him and lie across the corridor in
slanted beams, and each chandelier throws a visible warm cone downward through the mist. He passes through them one after another, so light slides slowly down his face and
shoulders and off again.
THE GLINTS. The air is full of drifting motes and tiny floating specks turning slowly in the beams, some rising rather than falling. The ones nearest the lens are far out of focus
and read as big soft round points of light; the ones inside the beams catch the chandeliers and bloom into small soft sparkling glints before drifting dark again. Each time he
crosses a beam the water on his skin and the drops in his hair do the same. All of it is physically suspended in the air and lit by the light already in the corridor — never drawn
on top of the picture, never symmetrical, never moving in a pattern and never trailing behind him.
THE GLOW. Strong soft bloom around every light source, the chandeliers halating into wide soft stars, the gilded mirrors and pale panelling glowing, the edges and corners of frame
diffused and milky, blacks lifted almost to grey. The image is soft overall while his face stays clearly readable from 02.0 onward and his eyes stay sharp inside the softness.
THE TIME. Motion runs at about 70% speed with smooth realistic blur, so bodies, water, hair, steam, mist and drifting glints all move heavy, late and velvety while he still covers
the whole distance inside the eight seconds.
No graphic overlays of any kind: no drawn stars, no cartoon twinkles, no glitter texture, no hearts, no lens flare streaks and no filters laid over the frame. Everything magical
in this dream is made of mist, steam, beams, suspended glinting particles, water, bloom, soft diffusion, shallow focus and slowed time.
WAKING LOOK — SHOTS 2 AND 3 ONLY
Instantly and completely different: clean, sharp, flat, ordinary, in focus edge to edge. Normal contrast, honest whites, no bloom, no halation, no diffusion, no soft focus, no
mist, no steam, no particles, no glow of any kind, full 100% speed. Both waking shots match each other exactly in grade, contrast and colour so the cut between them is invisible
as a look change and reads only as a change of angle. It should feel like the picture has been slapped awake at the same moment she has.

PHYSICS
HIS POSTURE THROUGHOUT THE DREAM: spine tall, chin level, shoulders open and back, free arm loose at his side, weight rolling smoothly from foot to foot in a long even unhurried
stride. None of it changes at any point.
The steam rolls out of the doorway with real volume and weight, spreads along the floor and rises, and thins as it travels. Water beads and runs slowly on his shoulders and drips
from the ends of his wet hair; each drop falls late and heavy. The towel hangs with real terry-cloth weight and swings a beat behind his stride, and the low mist swirls and parts
around his legs as he moves through it and closes again behind him. His wet strands stay stuck to his forehead. At the end he leans in from the hips and the spine with real weight
and no acceleration, his hands staying exactly where they are, and the frame tilts up slowly and settles rather than being knocked.
Her retreat has real body mechanics even though she is unseen: each backward step lands slightly heavily because she is not looking where she is going, giving the frame a small
vertical settle and a tiny sideways balance correction, and the pauses between the steps are uneven.
Awake, the bedding has real cloth behaviour: the duvet is genuinely twisted and heavy where it has been kicked, the sheet is rucked into folds under her, the throw lies crumpled on
the floor where it fell and the pillow is on its side on the floor. Her hair is authentically slept-in — flattened on one side, knotted and static-lifted on the other, some of it
stuck to her cheek. Her pyjamas are rucked and creased from a night of sleeping in them. The jolt is a real whole-body flinch that moves the mattress and the bedding with it. When
she bolts upright the mattress compresses and rebounds and her hair swings and settles late. When she shakes her head the hair whips across her face and keeps moving after her
head stops, her grip visibly gathers and tugs the hair at the roots, the mattress rocks under her and the loose duvet shifts with it, and everything comes to rest a beat after she
does.

LIGHTING
DREAM: warm concealed ceiling light and glowing chandeliers along the corridor, bright bloom off the mirrors and the pale panelling, and strong soft daylight from the arched
windows at the far end directly behind him, giving him a warm rim and creating the beams he walks through. Everything reads bright and washed toward white. His face stays clearly
readable once he is in the light and is the one clean point inside the soft image, with a bright catchlight in each eye.
WAKING: flat, plain early morning daylight through the thin white curtain from one side, cool and honest, filling the small room evenly, identical in both waking shots. From above,
the same daylight falls across the bed and the bedding without a hard shadow. The bedside lamp is still on and reads as a weak warm point the daylight has beaten. No hard shadows
on her face, no styling, no glow, no beauty smoothing, real skin texture with visible pores.

AUDIO
The soundtrack consists of exactly three things and nothing else: Enju's one internal line, Ryan's one line, and the sounds of the two places.
EVERYTHING IN THE DREAM ECHOES. For the whole of shot 1 every sound sits inside a long, soft, cavernous reverb, as if the corridor were far bigger than it looks — voices arrive
doubled and trailing, consonants smear, tails hang on and decay slowly, and everything sounds slightly distant and slightly underwater even when it is close. This applies to her
voice, his voice and every ambient sound without exception.
ENJU'S INTERNAL VOICE — FIXED CHARACTERISTICS. She speaks exactly one line in the whole segment, and it is in the dream. A seventeen-year-old girl's voice: light and youthful,
fairly high in pitch, thin and breathy rather than full, soft and unpolished — not a trained or actorly voice. Natural conversational English with a light Korean accent. She
speaks SLOWLY and QUIETLY, with air around the words, half-finishing the sentence and trailing off. This is wonder and confusion, not panic — she is not shrieking, not squealing
and not excited; she sounds like someone quietly amazed and completely unable to explain what she is looking at. Barely above a whisper, close and intimate, as if thought rather
than performed, and wrapped in the same long dream reverb. Never announced, never narrated, never the voice of an adult woman. Her line is never spoken aloud.
RYAN'S LINE. His single spoken word is warm, low, relaxed and unhurried, close to the lens and carrying the same long reverb.
THE DREAM PLACE. Almost nothing, because the corridor is empty: the soft hiss and roll of steam, water dripping slowly, and his unhurried footfalls arriving out of the white —
all of it echoing down a corridor that sounds far too large.
THE HARD CUT. At 08.0 s the echo stops dead. The reverb does not fade — it is gone in one frame, replaced by the dry, close, boxy acoustic of a small bedroom. That switch from
enormous echo to no echo at all is the sound of waking up. The second cut at 10.0 s changes nothing in the sound: the room acoustic, the alarm and her breathing run straight
across it.
THE ALARM AND THE ROOM. A cheap repeating electronic alarm clock beep. It cuts in faint and wrong underneath the last beat of the dream at about 07.5 s, grows through the lean-in,
and on the hard cut becomes loud, close, dry and in the room. It continues at that level to the last frame and is never switched off. With it, the honest close sound of a small
bedroom: bedding shifting, a mattress creaking, her breathing, a distant street outside the window.
THE WAKING SOUND. On the jolt at 08.0 there is one sharp involuntary intake of breath through the mouth, short and unvoiced, and nothing else. Her only voiced sound in the whole
segment is the single loud frustrated shout at 10.9-12.6 while her hands are in her hair — one burst, wordless, exasperated and embarrassed, not a scream of fear and not crying.
After it, only fast breathing that slowly steadies to the last frame.
Everything audible in this segment is either her one thought or a sound one of those two places would actually make. Nothing else is added to the mix.

STYLE
Modern Korean teen drama, live-action, natural skin texture with real pores on every face. The dream is a good dream — warm, soft, blurred, glowing and magical — dominated by
white: white mist and steam and blooming diffused light with glinting suspended particles, and pastel blue, blush pink, cream and gold showing softly through it. The waking is
white walls, honey oak, dusty pink and cool daylight. Clean digital capture with very light grain.

QUALITY
The dream is intentionally soft, and that softness is a controlled optical look — genuine diffusion and shallow depth of field, even and stable across all eight seconds — never
digital smear, never ghosting, never doubled edges and never a compression mush. Inside that softness his face and eyes stay clean and readable from 02.0 onward. Both waking shots
are sharp edge to edge. Stable picture, natural colours, controlled highlights even in the heavy white mist and bloom. The slowed dream carries smooth realistic motion blur on the
walk, the water, the hair, the steam and the drifting glints and stays temporally stable throughout; the return to full speed and full sharpness on the hard cut is a clean instant
change with no ramp artefacts. The breathing sway and the three backward retreating steps of the point-of-view shot are organic and never become shake, judder or wobble. Her jolt
and her head-shaking carry natural cinematic motion blur and then resolve into readable held poses — no strobing, no frame-blending and no stutter. Identity holds across all three
shots: the same face, hair, pyjamas and room from every angle, with no drift at either cut. Hands keep correct human anatomy with five fingers, including the hand holding the
towel closed and both hands gripping her hair. No duplicated limbs, no extra fingers, no unmotivated flicker in the light, no frame-skipping stutter. The dream image runs
completely unbroken from the first frame to the hard cut, with no eyelid closures and no interruptions of any kind.

SCENE CONTEXT
The opening of an episode. A girl is dreaming, and she is inside the dream looking out of her own eyes. The corridor of her school is full of mist and floating light. A door opens
and the boy she likes comes out of it straight from the shower, in a towel, and walks at her — and then keeps coming, closer and closer, while she backs away until she has
nowhere left to go. He leans in, and an alarm clock takes it away one moment before anything happens. Then she wakes with a jolt, sideways across her own bed. The dream is one
unbroken look through her eyes — soft, blurred, glowing and magical, with everything echoing; the waking is one unbroken ordinary shot, dry and sharp.

STRUCTURE — TWO SHOTS

THE WAKING is ONE SINGLE UNBROKEN SHOT lasting four seconds from across the bedroom at mattress height. Clean, sharp, dry, flat morning light, normal speed, no mist, no glow and
no softness.
The cut between them is hard and the change in look and sound is total.

THE CAMERA IS HER EYES — HOW TO MAKE THIS READ
This is the most important instruction in the prompt. The dream shot is not a tracking shot, not a handheld shot and not a shot of a person. It is her vision, and it must behave
like a head and a pair of eyes:
— HEIGHT. Locked at 1.6 m, her standing eye level, for the whole shot.
— MOTION WHILE STANDING. Not smooth and not mechanical. The frame breathes: a slow irregular sway and a very slight rise and fall in time with her breathing, plus tiny constant
micro-corrections, the way a real head never holds perfectly still. No dolly smoothness, no gimbal glide, no drone float.
— THE RETREAT. When she gives ground, the frame moves BACKWARD in two discrete uneven pushes, one per step, each with a small vertical bounce as her weight lands and a tiny
sideways wobble as her balance resets. It is a person walking backwards without looking, not a camera pulling back on rails. Between the steps the frame holds and breathes. The
retreat is never continuous and never even, and the second step is shorter than the first.
— LOOKING. When the frame turns, it turns the way a head turns: a small quick movement that arrives and settles, not a slow even pan.
— HER EYES STAY OPEN THE WHOLE TIME. The look is completely unbroken: her eyelids never close, nothing ever wipes, darkens, dips or interrupts the image, and the picture runs
continuously from the first frame to the hard cut at 06.0 s. The dream is one long unblinking look.
— NOBODY IS HER. No part of her body, her hands, her hair, her shoulders, her nose or her reflection is ever visible. She is not present in her own dream as a figure.
— EYELINE. Ryan looks INTO the lens, because the lens is her face. His eyes meet the camera and hold it.
— NOTHING IS BETWEEN THEM. There is no glass, no window, no screen, no mirror and no barrier of any kind between the camera and the corridor. The lens is her bare eyes in open
air. Nothing is ever tapped, knocked or pressed against a surface, and there is no reflection on the front of the image.
— NOTHING EVER TOUCHES HER. There is no physical contact anywhere in the shot. No hand, no arm and no finger ever enters the frame from any edge. He never reaches for her and
never holds her. He simply arrives in her space and leans in, and the only thing that changes in the frame is his face coming closer.
— THE FRAME TILTS UP AS HE COMES IN. As he arrives right in front of her and begins to lean, the whole image tilts upward five to seven degrees, smoothly and slowly, and stays
there. This is her own head tipping back to keep his face in view because he is taller and very close — it is her neck, not a camera move, and nothing causes it by touch. The
frame never jolts or shakes at any point.
There is no cut, no dissolve, no speed change and no reframe anywhere inside the dream shot.
