THE CAMERA IS HER EYES — HOW TO MAKE THIS READ
This is the most important instruction in the prompt. The dream shot is not a tracking shot, not a handheld shot and not a shot of a person. It is her vision, and it must behave
like a head and a pair of eyes:
— HEIGHT. Locked at 1.6 m, her standing eye level, for the whole shot.
— MOTION WHILE STANDING. Not smooth and not mechanical. The frame breathes: a slow irregular sway and a very slight rise and fall in time with her breathing, plus tiny constant
micro-corrections, the way a real head never holds perfectly still. No dolly smoothness, no gimbal glide, no drone float.
— THE RETREAT. When she gives ground, the frame moves BACKWARD in discrete uneven pushes, one per step, each with a small vertical bounce as her weight lands and a tiny sideways
wobble as her balance resets. It is a person walking backwards without looking, not a camera pulling back on rails. Between steps the frame holds and breathes. The retreat is
never continuous and never even.
— LOOKING. When the frame turns, it turns the way a head turns: a small quick movement that arrives and settles, not a slow even pan.
— HER EYES STAY OPEN THE WHOLE TIME. The look is completely unbroken: her eyelids never close, nothing ever wipes, darkens, dips or interrupts the image, and the picture runs
continuously from the first frame to the hard cut at 22.0 s. The dream is one long unblinking look.
— NOBODY IS HER. No part of her body, her hands, her hair, her shoulders, her nose or her reflection is ever visible. She is not present in her own dream as a figure.
— EYELINE. Ryan looks INTO the lens, because the lens is her face. His eyes meet the camera and hold it.
— NOTHING IS BETWEEN THEM. There is no glass, no window, no screen, no mirror and no barrier of any kind between the camera and the corridor. The lens is her bare eyes in open
air. Nothing is ever tapped, knocked or pressed against a surface, and there is no reflection on the front of the image.
— NOTHING EVER TOUCHES HER. There is no physical contact anywhere in the shot. No hand, no arm and no finger ever enters the frame from any edge. He never reaches for her and
never holds her. He simply arrives in her space and leans in, and the only thing that changes in the frame is his face coming closer.
— THE FRAME TILTS UP AS HE COMES IN. As he arrives right in front of her and begins to lean, the whole image tilts upward five to seven degrees, smoothly and slowly, and stays
there. This is her own head tipping back to keep his face in view because he is taller and very close — it is her neck, not a camera move, and nothing causes it by touch. The
frame never jolts or shakes at any point.
There is no cut, no dissolve, no speed change and no reframe anywhere inside the dream shot.

rather than records it. Focus is shallow and soft everywhere: the corridor, the lockers, the gilded mirrors, the chandeliers and the far end all sit in creamy defocus with soft

corners of the picture are softer than the centre, and the softness increases with distance until the far end of the corridor is nothing but glowing white. Highlights bleed

field — steady and even for all twenty-two seconds, never smear, never doubled edges, never ghosting and never digital blur.
THE MIST. Thick white mist fills the corridor from floor to ceiling, denser with distance until the far end is nothing but pale glowing white. A heavier layer lies along the floor
and rolls slowly. It never clears.
THE STEAM. The plain door releases a heavy, slow, rolling cloud of white steam that pours out at floor level, billows to head height and feeds into the mist. He walks out of that
cloud and it keeps trailing off his shoulders and his wet hair for the whole shot.

ACTING TASK — ENJU (fully invested; the work happens in her eyes)
SCENE DIRECTION (unspoken): survive being looked at this closely.
MOTIVE (her fuel): nobody has ever caught her before — not once, not at anything — and being held up like this in the middle of a full room is the most exposed she has been in
her life.
GOAL: understand what is on his face without letting him see what is on hers.
OBSTACLE: he is not looking away, she cannot get her own weight back under her, and she cannot make herself look away either.
TACTIC: she searches his face because she has to know what this is, and every answer sends her back for another — which is exactly why her eyes never settle. She is embarrassed
the whole way through, and the embarrassment is not funny to her and never turns into a laugh or a smile; she has no way to make it lighter, so she just endures it. When it
becomes too much she does the only thing available and drops her eyes — and lands on his throat, which tells her he is not calm either. That does not help. She leaves her hand
where it is until he lets go, because taking it away would be an admission that she noticed it.
Moment to moment:
— the settle in shot 1 — the fear goes out and something else comes in, and it arrives in her eyes before anywhere else
— shot 2, the big single — pure exposure; the searching is literal, eye to eye to mouth to eye, and the mouth stays closed
— the eyes dropping — not shyness played for charm, an actual retreat, and it happens because she has run out of ability to hold his gaze
— shot 5, her hand — she notices herself holding on and cannot make herself stop
— "Yeah — yeah, I'm okay. Thank you..." — the first word is for the room and the rest is for him; uneven, and the last word goes nowhere
(Safety: gaze always engaged in the task, never a frozen glassy stare; natural uneven blink cadence, constant live micro-movement of the pupils in the held shots, dry eyes with
no tears and no welling, and no smile, no laugh, no grin at any point.)

ACTING TASK — CHEN (fully invested; the work happens in his eyes)
SCENE DIRECTION (unspoken): do not let her see how much this just changed.
MOTIVE (his fuel): the catch was reflex; what he found out in the second after it was not, and it is far bigger than he was ready for.
GOAL: keep looking at her for as long as she lets him.
OBSTACLE: the moment he lets go it becomes a thing that happened instead of a thing that is happening, and if he smiles it becomes a joke.
TACTIC: he does not check the floor, the food or the room, because none of them matter as much as her face. He reads her continuously — the eyes keep moving because he keeps
finding new information. He deliberately does not smile: smiling would let them both off the hook and he does not want to be let off. Nothing about him performs. The only thing
that escapes him is his throat, twice, and he does not know it shows. He is the one who ends it, because ending it himself is the only way to keep it, and then he plays the
whole thing down and asks the flattest question he can find so she does not have to be embarrassed in front of anyone.
Moment to moment:
— the settle in shot 1 — the effort is real and his footing resets once, and he is already only looking at her
— shot 3, the swallow — involuntary; this is the tell he cannot control and the only sign that he is not steady
— shot 4, the big single — falling for her in real time, entirely in the eyes, with the rest of his face absolutely still and unsmiling
— shot 6, his hand — relaxed, not gripping; he is holding her up, not holding on, and the one small thumb movement is the whole of what he allows himself
— the release — deliberate and unhurried, and he does it first
— "You okay?" — level and easy, pitched to make it small
— he never once looks off-frame at the spilled food, at the room or toward Jenny
(Safety: gaze always engaged, never a frozen glassy stare; natural uneven blink cadence, constant live micro-movement of the pupils in the held shots, dry eyes, and no smile,
no smirk, no laugh at any point.)

ACTING TASK — JENNY (fully invested; the work happens in her eyes)
SCENE DIRECTION (unspoken): she has just watched her own plan hand him a reason to hold the girl.
MOTIVE (her fuel): she wanted the new girl on the floor with her food in her lap in front of everyone, and instead she has made her the most interesting person in the room,

GOAL: keep looking at him, because she cannot make herself stop.
OBSTACLE: it is happening a metre in front of her and there is nothing she can do about it from a chair.

— the first look — not confusion, not calculation: raw jealousy, aimed at him specifically
— the anger arriving behind it — jaw, brows, a hard breath in; the feeling gets bigger, not smaller

ACTING TASK — RYAN (fully invested; the work happens in his eyes, his jaw and his hand)

(Safety: gaze always engaged in a task, never a frozen glassy stare; natural uneven blink cadence in both long-lens shots, dry eyes with no tears and no welling. Anger held in

ACTING TASK — ENJU (fully invested; the work happens in her eyes)
SCENE DIRECTION (unspoken): survive being looked at this closely.
MOTIVE (her fuel): nobody has ever caught her before — not once, not at anything — and being held up like this in the middle of a full room is the most exposed she has been in
her life.
GOAL: understand what is on his face without letting him see what is on hers.
OBSTACLE: he is not looking away, she cannot get her own weight back under her, and she cannot make herself look away either.
TACTIC: she searches his face because she has to know what this is, and every answer sends her back for another — which is exactly why her eyes never settle. She is embarrassed
the whole way through, and the embarrassment is not funny to her and never turns into a laugh or a smile; she has no way to make it lighter, so she just endures it. When it
becomes too much she does the only thing available and drops her eyes — and lands on his throat, which tells her he is not calm either. That does not help. She leaves her hand
where it is until he lets go, because taking it away would be an admission that she noticed it.
Moment to moment:
— the settle in shot 1 — the fear goes out and something else comes in, and it arrives in her eyes before anywhere else
— shot 2, the big single — pure exposure; the searching is literal, eye to eye to mouth to eye, and the mouth stays closed
— the eyes dropping — not shyness played for charm, an actual retreat, and it happens because she has run out of ability to hold his gaze
— shot 5, her hand — she notices herself holding on and cannot make herself stop
— "Yeah — yeah, I'm okay. Thank you..." — the first word is for the room and the rest is for him; uneven, and the last word goes nowhere
(Safety: gaze always engaged in the task, never a frozen glassy stare; natural uneven blink cadence, constant live micro-movement of the pupils in the held shots, dry eyes with
no tears and no welling, and no smile, no laugh, no grin at any point.)

eventually come and correct.
GOAL: find out what she has done wrong before she has to walk into that room.
OBSTACLE: she cannot think of anything, which is much worse than being able to.
TACTIC: she searches faces — first her friends (<<<image_5>>>), genuinely hunting for one person who knows why, then the corridor as she walks, catching the few students who turn away a
half-second too late. Every face that gives her nothing confirms something she does not yet have a word for. Her hand on the strap of <<<image_3>>> is doing the only thing her hands can
do.
Moment to moment:
— in the huddle — warm, quick, enjoying being the one with the story, and slightly careful with it, the way somebody is when being included is still new.
— the bell — she looks up at the speaker the way anyone would, calm and mildly curious, fully expecting it to be about somebody else.
— the announcement — she listens to the whole of it properly and does not react while it is playing. The stillness is real, not braced.
— the arms unfolding — the first thing her body does about it, and she does not notice herself doing it.
— "Me? Why?" — asked of her friends, quietly. The second word is the one she actually needs answered.
— reading the three of them — one, two, three, and the third one's fading smile is the one that finishes her. She does not wait around after it; there is nothing left to ask.
— the walk down the corridor — she does not hurry and she does not look back, and holding that costs her everything she has.
— the knob — she does not hesitate twice. She has decided, and the hand turns and the body goes forward in one movement.

roughly evenly spaced, close enough that they are plainly one group and not four people who happen to be near each other. ENJEE stands on the FAR side of the circle from camera so
that she faces toward the lens across it and her face reads clearly; the friend on the near side of the circle is seen mostly from behind and over the shoulder. The circle stays a
circle for the whole first half of the part — nobody steps out of it, nobody lines up shoulder to shoulder and nobody turns out toward camera. Students pass around the outside of the
group in both directions the whole time.
THEIR BUSINESS IS ORDINARY AND HANDS-ON, WITH NO SCREENS: one girl is retying the ribbon in another girl's hair, that second girl is standing patiently with her chin lifted, the
third is holding two schoolbooks against her chest and talking with one free hand, and Enjee is telling them something. NOBODY IN THIS SEQUENCE HOLDS, LOOKS AT OR USES A PHONE OR
ANY OTHER SCREEN, in the circle or anywhere in the corridor, at any point.

ACTING TASK — ENJEE (fully invested in her tactic; the work happens in her eyes)
SCENE DIRECTION (shared, unspoken): get through this corridor without becoming an event.
MOTIVE (her fuel): three weeks ago nobody looked at her at all, and some part of her has been quietly waiting for the visibility to turn out to be a mistake somebody would
eventually come and correct.
GOAL: find out what she has done wrong before she has to walk into that room.
OBSTACLE: she cannot think of anything, which is much worse than being able to.
TACTIC: she searches faces. It starts as an ordinary check of her friends — genuinely hunting for one person who knows why, reading each of the three in turn and adjusting as she
gets nothing — and then it becomes a scan of the corridor as she walks, catching the students who turn away a half-second too late. Every face that gives her nothing confirms
something she does not yet have a word for. Her hand on the strap is doing the only thing her hands can do.
Moment to moment:
— in the circle — warm, quick, slightly careful; she checks after her own joke whether it landed, the way she always has.
— the chime — she turns her head toward the speaker like anyone would, unhurried, expecting it to be about somebody else.
— the announcement — she listens to the whole of it properly, with her whole attention, and does not react while it is playing.
— afterwards — she reacts a full beat later, once she has checked the name against herself.
— "…Me?" — asked of her friends, quietly, and genuinely a question.
— reading the three of them — one, two, three, and the third one's fading smile is the one that finishes her.
— the two seconds of thinking — she is running through everything she has done this week and finding nothing. This is real cognitive work and it shows in her eyes, not in her face:
no performed worry, no lip bite, no bracing.
— the walk — she does not hurry and she does not look back, and holding that costs her everything she has.
— the door — the breath is not brave. It is a girl gathering herself in a corridor where everyone can see her doing it.
(Safety: gaze always engaged in the task — never a frozen, glassy stare; natural blink cadence, including through the two seconds of thinking.)

ACTING TASK — THE THREE FRIENDS
They are not cold and they are not conspirators — they simply do not know anything, and none of them is quick enough to offer to walk with her before the moment has passed. Each
gives a different real answer: the shrug is honest bewilderment, the head-shake is sympathy without information, and the fading smile is the one who has understood that this is
serious about a second before the others do. After she leaves, they look at each other rather than after her.

ACTING TASK — the scene
SCENE DIRECTION (shared, unspoken): let nothing here look like anything.

ACTING TASK — ENJEE (fully invested in her tactic; the work happens in her eyes)
MOTIVE (her fuel): nobody has ever done anything like this for her, and for about four seconds she lets herself have it.
GOAL: find out who did this and what it says — and then get all of it out of sight before anybody makes it a thing.
OBSTACLE: she is standing in a public corridor, and attention has never once been safe for her.
TACTIC: first she reads the gifts, then she reads the room, and the second one wins.
Moment to moment:
— the avalanche: pure reflex, protect the head and the book. No performed scream and no falling over.
— the look: her eyes actually work — they move object to object across the pile, taking inventory, and each one makes it slightly less possible that this is a prank. This is where
the audience falls in love with her.
— "Oooh..." — small, warm, half laughed, entirely to herself. Not a squeal and not for anybody's benefit, but genuinely delighted.
— the card: she wants to know who. Turning the envelope over to look at the handwriting is the most honest thing she does in the scene.
— the check left and right: this is the acting task made visible. The looking IS the doing — her eyes move from one cluster to the next, hunting for a face that is enjoying this.
She finds two or three heads turned her way and that is enough. Nobody actually laughs at her; she talks herself out of it.
— clearing it up: fast, embarrassed, competent. The warmth is gone and she is hiding evidence of it.
— she never touches the backpack and never looks at it. She is busy, not oblivious, and that is why she misses everything.
— "Okay..." — spoken to herself as the locker shuts, the sound of a girl ticking a task off a list.
(Safety: gaze engaged and moving with the task, never a frozen unfocused stare; natural blink cadence.)

ACTING TASK — JENNY (fully invested in her tactic; the work happens in her eyes)
MOTIVE (her fuel): she needs Enjee gone, and just as much she needs to be a person who did not do this.
GOAL: cross this corridor exactly like somebody who is only crossing a corridor.
OBSTACLE: the one second where her hand is doing something her face has to pretend it is not.
TACTIC: she gives her eyes a job that is not Enjee — the classroom door at the far end of the corridor — and holds it, so that nothing in her face is available to read.
Moment to moment:
— the walk in: ordinary, unhurried, already committed. She worked out the mechanics before she got here, which is why her hand needs no aiming.
— passing Enjee: her eyes stay locked forward on the door. The discipline is the performance — no glance down, no glance sideways, no visible held breath.
— the small smile four steps later: the only leak in the whole sequence, and it is for herself, not for anyone watching.
(Safety: gaze engaged on her chosen point ahead, never a frozen unfocused stare; natural blink cadence.)

centimetre on polished stone. Her crouch loads onto the balls of her feet with one hand out for balance. Skirt ruffles and hair swing a beat late on the flinch and again on every
turn. The loaded canvas backpack rides on her shoulders with real weight, the soft fabric creasing along the seams and the straps pulling as she moves; it never comes off her back.

locker — so nobody in the frame is ever frozen.

SCENE CONTEXT
Night, the bench outside the dormitory. The film opens on a slow push-in onto the two of them, which eases out and settles. Enjee is already working on the graze on Ryan's cheek with a cotton bud, holding his jaw steady with her other hand. He apologises WHILE she works — two short sentences, one straight after the other, for keeping the truth about his family from her — and it costs him: he is ashamed, his head moves in a small slow shake at himself as he says it, and his voice thickens. She does not stop; she keeps treating the wound and keeps glancing up from it to his eyes. She gives the graze one last touch, takes both hands away from his face, looks at him and answers in one flat sentence. He nods. A short beat. Then the corner of her mouth goes and she adds a condition that lets them both out of it — and he raises it, completely straight-faced. Eighteen seconds, one location, eleven timed shots. Voices and sound effects only; no music.

OPENING CAMERA MOVE — A SLOW PUSH-IN, AT A CALM SPEED
The film opens on ONE SMOOTH PUSH-IN LASTING ABOUT ONE AND TWO-TENTHS SECONDS. The camera starts about 3.2 metres from the bench, holding the two of them a little loose in frame with the steps and the hedge around them, and TRAVELS FORWARD IN A STRAIGHT LINE TOWARD THEM until it is about 2 metres out, where the move eases to a stop on the two-shot. The lens does not change — this is a real dolly move forward, not a zoom, so the perspective deepens naturally as it travels.
IT IS A CALM, EVEN, UNHURRIED PUSH at an ordinary cinematic speed — gentle acceleration at the start, a soft ease-out at the end. IT IS NOT A WHIP, NOT A SNAP, NOT A LUNGE AND NOT FAST. THE PICTURE STAYS COMPLETELY SHARP AND READABLE THROUGHOUT — the bench, both faces and her hands at his cheek are clear the whole way in. There is no streaking, no smear and no motion-blur effect.
THIS IS A PICTURE-ONLY MOVE. THE SOUNDTRACK DOES NOT CHANGE FOR IT AT ALL — the ordinary night ambience runs at a constant level from the very first frame, straight through the push and onward. There is no whoosh, no swish, no air movement, no riser, no impact and no transition sound effect of any kind.
FROM 1.2 SECONDS ONWARD THE CAMERA IS COMPLETELY LOCKED OFF. The push exists only at the head of the film and never returns; there is no further camera movement, drift, sway, pan or push anywhere in the rest of the film.

SPEECH RATE — THE MOST IMPORTANT RULE IN THIS FILM
There are only five short lines in eighteen seconds, and each one has been given more time than it needs. EVERY WORD IS FULLY PRONOUNCED AT A CALM, DELIBERATE, CONVERSATIONAL SPEAKING RATE — roughly three to four syllables per second, the pace of someone speaking carefully to one person sitting close to them. Every syllable is audible and every word is clearly articulated.
Approximate length of each line as spoken:
— "I'm sorry I hid the truth about my family." takes ABOUT THREE AND A HALF SECONDS.
— "It was wrong." takes ABOUT ONE SECOND.
— "Okay. Just don't hide things from me again." takes ABOUT THREE SECONDS.
— "And you're buying me lunch. For a week." takes ABOUT TWO AND A HALF SECONDS.
— "Two weeks." takes ABOUT ONE SECOND.
NO LINE IS EVER COMPRESSED, SPED UP, CLIPPED OR SQUEEZED TO FIT. If a line needs a moment more, the silence around it gives way — the words never do. Nobody gabbles, nobody rushes, nobody swallows the ends of words.

EMOTION SLOWS HIM DOWN, IT DOES NOT SPEED HIM UP
Ryan is emotional and guilty when he apologises — and guilt makes a person speak MORE SLOWLY, not faster. The feeling weighs his words down. His voice is low and a little thick, the breath is not quite steady, and each word comes out heavier and slower than his normal speech. He is not agitated and he is not in a hurry to get it over with.

HIS HEAD MOVES WHILE HE SPEAKS — GUILT
As he says the apology he gives A SMALL, SLOW SHAKE OF THE HEAD — a few degrees left and right, twice, aimed at himself, the way someone does when they cannot believe what they did. His eyes drop from hers for a moment on the shake and come back up. His jaw is tight, his throat works once before he starts, and his eyebrows pull slightly together in the middle. Because Enjee's hand is under his jaw, HER HAND MOVES WITH HIM and then steadies him again — she adjusts her grip a fraction to keep the bud on the wound. The head movement is small and controlled, never a big theatrical swing.

Enjee's complexion is ONE SMOOTH EVEN TONE from hairline to jaw and down the neck — uniform, unbroken, healthy, flawless. Both of her cheeks are exactly the same clean colour as her forehead and her chin: smooth, matte, untouched skin all the way across. Her hands are clean. The ointment, the shine and the injury belong to Ryan's right cheekbone alone and appear nowhere else in the film.

RYAN'S CARDIGAN IS CLEAN
The pale blue ribbed cardigan is ONE EVEN, UNIFORM PALE BLUE across the entire garment — left shoulder, right shoulder, both sleeves, chest and back are all exactly the same fresh clean shade, as if it came straight out of the wardrobe. The white shirt collar and cuffs are crisp white. The wool colour is continuous and consistent everywhere.

RYAN'S TWO SENTENCES RUN STRAIGHT ON
His apology is two sentences said one after the other as a single continuous thought. BETWEEN THEM THERE IS ONLY A BREATH — under half a second. He does not stop, does not search for the words and does not sit thinking between the two lines. He already knows what he is going to say; he says it, and then he stops.

Nine of the eleven shots are TIGHT SINGLES ON ONE FACE; there is one two-shot at the start and one at the end, and nothing else is wider. HER REACTION IS COVERED AS MUCH AS HIS WORDS — the camera cuts to Enjee's face DURING his apology, not only after it. No two adjacent shots are the same size.

ACTING TASK — RYAN (fully invested in his tactic; the work happens in his eyes)
SCENE DIRECTION (shared, unspoken): put this right tonight, on this bench, before either of them goes inside.
MOTIVE (his fuel): she is cleaning a wound he got because of his own mess, and she did not ask a single question before doing it. She has known him a year and never knew who his family are, because he decided she shouldn't.
GOAL: be forgiven — not let off, forgiven.
OBSTACLE: he is ashamed of himself, and she is looking at his cheek and not at him — and the three times she does look, he loses his footing.
TACTIC: he says it while she is working precisely because she is working. He has the words ready and gets them out in one go, short and slow, without explaining himself — an explanation would turn into an excuse. Two sentences, straight through, and then he stops and lets her decide.

— before the first word — the throat works once; the jaw is tight; the eyebrows pull slightly in.
— "I'm sorry I hid the truth about my family." — low, thick, heavy, EVERY WORD FULLY SPOKEN; the guilt makes it slow.
— the head shake on "hid" — small, slow, at himself; the eyes drop and come back.
— THE FIRST GLANCE — the breath catches; he does not look away.
— straight on — one breath and the second sentence follows immediately; no thinking pause.
— "It was wrong." — smaller and plainer still, and slower; no excuse after it; then he stops for good.
— the second head shake, in silence — slower than the first, eyes down, then up to her.
— THE SECOND GLANCE — he sees something move in her and cannot read it.
— the waiting — he says nothing and does not fill the silence.
— THE THIRD GLANCE — it lands hardest; he holds it as long as she does.
— her hands coming away — the verdict arriving.
— "…don't hide things from me again." — the nod; no defence; something loosens in his chest.
— the lunch line — a short beat of not expecting it; the breath goes out of him.

SCENE DIRECTION (shared, unspoken): keep the show going — it's a party, everything is fun.

SCENE CONTEXT
Night, at the backyard pool — the same moment as the episode's opening hook, now with its ending. Jenny watches Chen, Enjee
and Ryan laughing together on the back porch and sips her poison-red punch. An over-excited guest in a horse mask dances past
and bumps her into the pool — the same fall, the same red water, the same panicked guests. Then Jenny bursts up through the
surface, soaked and furious, and the whole party bursts out laughing.
